news.title: Researchers build the first ever quantum clock that uses sunlight
paras: Facebook Threads X / Twitter WhatsApp LinkedIn Reddit Email Print The sun, as captured by the ESA/NASA Solar Orbiter mission ESA & NASA/Solar Orbiter/EUI Team, E. Kraaikamp (ROB) For the first time, researchers have built a quantum clock that uses light from the sun as a key component.

It could be used to diagnose shifts in the sun’s velocity or probe processes on its surface. People have known that they can keep track of time with sunlight ever since antiquity. But contemporary record-breaking timekeepers, which are called optical clocks , derive their accuracy from quantum mechanical effects and typically have atoms that have been isolated from the external world at their core.

news.title: In elephants, the resilience of communities has its limits
paras: Network problems In elephants, the resilience of communities has its limits In Sri Lanka, ecological change is shrinking a park’s elephant population. Individuals die or move away, calves grow up, and newcomers join, but the local communities as a whole usually hold together.

Long-term studies of African savanna elephants have shown that, even after poaching or other spikes in deaths, survivors tend to rebuild their lost connections over time. But a new study suggests that resilience may not keep the community intact when steady losses accumulate over time. Anastasia Madsen, a behavioral ecologist at the University of California, San Diego, and her colleagues analyzed 12 years of observations of wild Asian elephants in Sri Lanka.

news.title: Astronomers trace mystery radio signals back to cosmic odd couple of white dwarf and sun-like star
paras: "It’s amazing that by using radio wavelengths, we can detect the storms on a star over 5,000 light-years away." The white dwarf in the newly discovered system, designated GPM J071507−114153 and located around 5,000 light-years away, spins once every eight minutes, sending out radio pulses.

These radio pulses have been seen from binary systems with smaller and cooler red dwarf stars before, but rarely from a system like GPM J071507−114153. GPM J071507−114153 belongs to a class of celestial objects called long-period transients (LPTs) known to produce radio signals that switch on and off over intervals of minutes or hours.

For more than two centuries, historians discredited the idea that the Roman-era artifact came from Scotland, instead assuming that it was hacked off a monument in England and hauled north by marauding tribes. Instead, they posit that it formed part of a colossal equestrian statue of the Roman Emperor Antoninus Pius that once stood in southern Scotland in the second century C.E., before it was dismantled by retreating Roman troops.
